blocks.content: Paging solves fragmentation, but it introduces a real cost: every single memory access now needs an extra step just to translate the address. The TLB is the hardware trick that makes that cost disappear almost entirely.
1. The Performance Problem Paging Introduces

Naive paging requires an actual memory access to the page table just to translate a logical address into a physical one. That means every memory access a program makes actually costs TWO real memory accesses.

One access looks up the page table entry to find the right frame. A second access then fetches the actual data from that frame. This effectively doubles memory access time compared to a system with no translation at all.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408865182-753022283.png
2. The TLB: A Cache for Translations
blocks.text: 2. The TLB: A Cache for Translations

blocks.content: The Translation Lookaside Buffer, TLB, is a small, extremely fast, dedicated hardware cache built directly into the CPU. It stores a handful of the MOST RECENTLY USED page number to frame number translations.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408865182-140129742.png
blocks.alt: The TLB: A Cache for Translations

blocks.content: 3. TLB Hit vs TLB Miss
When the CPU generates a logical address, it first checks the TLB. If the needed page number is found there, a TLB HIT, the frame number is retrieved instantly with no memory access at all.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408865182-192962148.png

If the page number is not in the TLB, a TLB MISS, the CPU falls back to the slower full page table lookup in memory. Critically, that result is then also stored into the TLB, so the same page will hit next time.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408865183-974393597.png
4. Worked Example: Tracing Hits and Misses
blocks.text: 4. Worked Example: Tracing Hits and Misses

blocks.content: Consider a small TLB and a sequence of page accesses: 3, 3, 7, 3, 9, 7. The first access to page 3 is a miss, it gets cached. The second access to page 3 is now a hit. Page 7 is a fresh miss and gets cached. The next page 3 access is a hit again. Page 9 is a new miss. The final page 7 access hits, since it was cached earlier.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408967921-86743801.png
blocks.alt: Worked Example: Tracing Hits and Misses

blocks.content: 5. Why This Works So Well: Locality of Reference
blocks.text: 5. Why This Works So Well: Locality of Reference

blocks.content: Programs tend to access the same small set of pages repeatedly over a short period of time rather than jumping randomly across their entire address space. This behavioral pattern is called locality of reference.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408967923-80579912.png
blocks.alt: Why This Works So Well: Locality of Reference

blocks.title: Why a tiny cache can work so well
blocks.content: The TLB only needs to hold a handful of entries, yet real systems commonly see hit ratios of 98 percent or higher, precisely because of locality.
6. Computing Effective Memory Access Time
Given a hit ratio, a hit access time, and a miss access time, the effective access time is a weighted average of the two paths.
{"headers":["Scenario","Time"],"rows":[["TLB hit access time","10 nanoseconds"],["TLB miss access time (extra page table lookup)","100 nanoseconds"],["Hit ratio","98 percent"]]}

effective time = (0.98 * 10) + (0.02 * 100)
             = 9.8 + 2.0
             = 11.8 nanoseconds

At a 98 percent hit ratio, the effective access time of 11.8 nanoseconds is barely worse than a pure 10 nanosecond hit, even though a miss costs ten times more. This is the direct payoff of a high hit ratio.
7. What Happens on a Context Switch
blocks.text: 7. What Happens on a Context Switch

blocks.content: TLB entries belong to one specific process's page table. Once a different process starts running, those cached translations are no longer valid, since the same page number in a different process maps to a completely different frame.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408967925-409160663.png
blocks.alt: What Happens on a Context Switch

blocks.content: The simplest fix is to flush, clear, the entire TLB on every context switch, guaranteeing correctness at the cost of every process starting with a cold, empty TLB. A more modern hardware approach tags each entry with a process identifier so multiple processes' entries can coexist safely without confusion.

9. Common Mistakes

["Assuming the TLB stores actual DATA, when it only stores address TRANSLATIONS, page number to frame number mappings.","Forgetting the TLB needs to be flushed or otherwise invalidated on a context switch, or it would return WRONG translations belonging to a different process."]
items: Assuming the TLB stores actual DATA, when it only stores address TRANSLATIONS, page number to frame number mappings.
Forgetting the TLB needs to be flushed or otherwise invalidated on a context switch, or it would return WRONG translations belonging to a different process.

blocks.content: 10. Interview Angle

Being able to compute an effective memory access time given a hit ratio, a hit time, and a miss time, is one of the most common OS interview and exam calculations. Practice it until the weighted average formula feels automatic.
